content:
I wanted to ask a question and I'm not sure where the best place for it is - I'm going to put it here in the hope that general is as good as anywhere.

I don't know what I'm going to do next. In about 11 months, my current funding peters out - with redundancy etc., I'll need a new job secured to start by the beginning of next summer. This isn't me trying to sell myself. In truth I don't understand how to do that. But I know I am not without skills. I have a PhD in formal verification of cryptography; I have been learning Lean for 6 years and actively contributing to Mathlib for a good part of that; I am not stupid or incapable. I'm not sure I want to move - I don't know if I can face that disruption again, or the financial strain of it. But otherwise I don't think I'm a bad prospect.

I don't understand - I don't see - how to create a personal path forward for myself, to find a sustainable way to be. I don't think I can cope with the anxiety of a temporary contract position paid by the hour. But I worry I'm too underpublished, too old, too autistic, to really hustle and hustle in the way that is required to make a place for myself.

Nobody else can solve this problem for me but me. But I would like to say that I would like advice. What is the path forward? Is there any hope, would you say? Or should I break my heart and just try to find a job, any job, even if it's in a supermarket stacking shelves? I worry that my heart will not be able to leave Lean and formalisation behind. It's troubling. I feel, well, troubled. I would appreciate something - any kind words of advice - that might relieve that.

Wrenna -- I don't suppose I have any wise words of wisdom to share, not least of which ones which make the real problems you're wrestling with go away -- but I can offer finding some time for a chat to think through ideas together, more than happy to. I suspect other (wiser or at least more adjacent career-wise) community members might be happy to offer the same if you think it'd be worthwhile. Feel free to DM me if you'd like, or I dare say to DM someone you value in the community and ask them if they care to do the same.

I think the actual situation isn't as bad as you imagine. The conditions of not wanting hourly work and refusing to relocate mean that a company would have to fully accept you working remotely. For some traditional types of businesses, this might be hard to accept, but it's not uncommon in software/internet companies.

Over the past year or two, we've seen several startups trying to integrate LLMs (or other AI solutions) with Lean (or other proof assistants). These startups, through clever promotion, have attracted significant investment and are actively hiring relevant people.

At the same time, Lean itself enjoys higher recognition among mathematicians (even though this doesn't necessarily mean Lean is better suited for formalizing mathematics). More and more mathematicians are participating in this model: collaborating with computer engineers, under some form of funding, to formalize key mathematical theorems.

"Startups trying to improve LLMs' mathematical capabilities" and "collaborative models within the mathematics community" are unlikely to disappear in the coming years (I think for even longer). I believe these are opportunities worth considering.

I wouldn't mind a job in the area - I already commute an hour and a half for work when I'm in the office (which is at least half a usual week). For some reason South Wales isn't yet a hub of AI verification though, yeah :P

It might be good to do a values assessment: determine what things are important to you for which you will accept no compromise, and other things to which you would acquiesce for sufficient inducement. You have partly done that above: I recommend revisiting the issues over the next few weeks as you plan for your future.

One possible pivot is to advertise as a consultant: start your own business and promote your specialty to companies that may have interest in your specialty. This will require some salespersonship and possibly be out of your comfort zone, but will allow you to develop many things on your own terms (which seems to me to be important to you). Use your current network to find and expand your network: look for potential contracts and others who already consult and see what you can learn with them. It isn't hustling if it is enabling you to do what you want, but it may involve more action and willingness to fail than spending the next 11 months trying to find a near-dream job; don't find it -- make it.

Good luck to you.
sender_full_name: J. J. Issai (project started by GRP)

content: Thank you. I really appreciate the honest advice.
